nodes.question: Why have urban exploiters thrived in urban areas?
nodes.answer: They have thrived due to landscape scale modifications to vegetation profiles and an excess of waste and rubbish produced by humans.
nodes.paragraph: However, Humphrey et al. (2023) characterised the same species as an urban adaptor in Melbourne. Australian white ibis (Threskiornis moluccus) (McKiernan and Instone 2016; Allatson and Connor 2018), several species of crow or raven and perhaps even the Australian magpie (Gym- norhina tibicen) (Humphrey et al. 2023) are consistently considered exploiters in urban areas. These exploiters have not just survived, but thrived, in urban areas; mostly as a result of landscape scale modification to vegetation profiles and our ability to produce an excess of waste and rubbish (Auman et al. 2011; Taylor et al. 2013). Urban adaptors on the other hand are not as adept at exploiting the urban environment and may include: fairywrens, medium sized parrots such as rosellas, and many raptor species (Parsons et al. 2008; Head- land et al. 2023; Humphrey et al. 2023). These birds can survive in urban settings, espe- cially older suburbs with mature vegetation. nodes.question: What role does vegetation play in urban bird species' survival?
nodes.answer: Vegetation quantity, structure, and composition are fundamental elements in urban areas that favor many bird species, with woodland cover helping sustain different forest species within cities.
nodes.paragraph: 2014 ; Villase or and Escobar 2019 ). However, these changes are also linked to other factors like the level of urbanization, or the pres - ence of certain traits related with the survival of birds in urban environments (Patankar et al. 2021 ). Also, at higher levels of urbanization, a decrease in similarity can be found between urban and non-urban areas because the increasing levels of urbanization enhance the differences between both extremes (Garaffa et al. 2009 ). Habitat loss or fragmentation effects on some urban birds are associated with the type of peri-urban matrix because woodland cover helps to sustain different forest species within cities (Hedblom and S derstr m 2010 ; Dale 2018 ). Thus, vegetation quantity, structure, and composition have been identified as fundamental elements in urban areas to be favorable to many bird species (Chace and Walsh 2006 ; Donnelly and Marzluff 2006 ; Gariz bal-Carmona and Mancera-Rodr guez 2021 ). nodes.question: What ecosystems are present in the city of Xalapa?
nodes.answer: The city of Xalapa has differing ecosystems, including pine-oak forests to the North and cloud forests to the South.
nodes.paragraph: 2005 ; De Toledo et al. 2012 ; Kor nyi et al. 2021 ). However, some bird species benefit from the presence of different urban features such as buildings, urban waste, or lawns, which offer an appropriate habitat for species associated with open and disturbed areas (White et al. 2005 ; Mainwaring 2015 ; Garc a-Arroyo et al. 2023 ). Furthermore, human food provisioning has been identified as a key factor related to bird presence in urban green areas, especially in places where natural resources are scarce, or their availability is limited by seasonality (Fern ndez-Juricic and Jokim ki 2001 ; Chamberlain et al. 2007 ; MacGregor-Fors 2022 ). In this study, we focused on understanding the role of the non-urban bird communities in a Neotropical city (Xalapa, Veracruz, Mexico) with differing ecosystems: pine-oak for - ests to the North and cloud forests to the South.
